docs.title: nolainquery
docs.text:
nolainquery answers questions about a file that already lives on your computer. You type something like “What is total revenue by country?”, and you get a table — and, if you asked for one, a chart — computed from that file.

The unusual part is where the work happens. Your file never leaves your machine. A remote service sees only a sketch of the data: column names, types, a few sample rows. It returns a recipe — executable analysis, and optionally a computation graph and a chart contract. Your computer runs that recipe against the real file. The numbers you see are true because they were computed locally, not because a model claimed them.

This documentation is for people who want to use, evaluate, understand, or integrate with nolainquery. Choose the route that matches your goal; each route starts with the least context it requires.

docs.title: Use nolainquery
docs.text:
1. Follow Using nolainquery to create an account, add an API key, and ask a first question.
  2. Use the local first-run guide when you want to run the desktop app from this repository.
  3. Continue with desktop workflows for common tasks.
  4. Check Credits before estimating usage. The troubleshooting guide covers common user-facing failures.

If you only have twenty minutes, read this page, Using nolainquery, and the opening of How nolainquery is built.

docs.title: Understand nolainquery
docs.text:
Start with How nolainquery is built for the privacy split and the principles behind it. Then read The parts of the system for component responsibilities and A conversation from start to finish for one representative end-to-end flow.

After that foundation, use Clarifications and How a Plan is declared to examine two deeper mechanisms. Query costs provides measured behavior rather than architectural intent.

docs.text:
Read Calling the Cloud API for the public HTTP contract, authentication requirements, endpoints, and request examples. The sketch and metadata contract is the focused reference for constructing the compact file description sent to the cloud.

API integrators do not need maintainer access or the private operational documentation.

docs.title: A few words you will meet again
docs.text:
Here is some glossary you will find useful to browse through the documentation.

Word Meaning in this book Sketch A compact description of a local file: columns, types, summaries, sample values. This is all the cloud is allowed to see. Artifact Something the cloud produces for the desktop to use: executable analysis, an optional computation graph, an optional chart contract. Capability A product the cloud knows how to generate. Today there is one: descriptive analysis of a single file. Plan An engine for a Capability — the sequence of steps that produces artifacts. Today the implemented engine is Pandas. Intent What kind of conversational turn this is (answer from the sketch, refuse, ask a clarifying question, or generate analysis). Not a product. Credits The unit you pay in. Each call to a language model settles immediately.

docs.title: Ask your first question with nolainquery
docs.text: nolainquery combines a desktop application with a hosted reasoning service called the Cloud API. The desktop reads a file on your computer, sends the Cloud API a compact description of that file, and runs the returned analysis locally. This guide takes you from sign-in to an observable answer.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the nolainquery desktop app running; to build it from the public repository, follow Try nolainquery locally
  • a Google account for portal sign-in
  • a positive credit balance
  • one local .csv or .parquet file

The preprocessing layer also implements .xlsx and .xls, but the current desktop file chooser exposes only CSV and Parquet. Excel is therefore not part of the supported desktop first-use path yet.

docs.title: Create an account and API key
docs.text:
The portal is the website where you sign in, view your balance, and manage API keys. An API key authorizes the desktop to use the Cloud API and spend credits from your account, so treat it like a password.

  1. Open nolainquery.com/login.
  2. Choose Continue with Google and complete sign-in.
  3. In Account → API Keys, optionally enter a label such as Laptop, then choose Create key.
  4. Copy the new key immediately. The full value is shown only once; store it in a password manager.

The portal supports up to five active keys. If a key is lost, revoke it in Account → API Keys and create a replacement.

docs.title: Connect the desktop
docs.text:
1. Open Settings in the desktop sidebar.
  2. Paste the key into API Key.
  3. Choose Save API Key.

The desktop validates the key against the Cloud API. Success is visible as a status badge showing the remaining credit balance and account tier. The key is stored on this device and sent to the Cloud API only to authenticate requests.

If the badge reports a missing, invalid, or zero-credit key, use the matching steps in Troubleshooting before continuing.

docs.title: Open a file and ask
docs.text:
1. Open Home and choose Choose dataset.
  2. Select a .csv or .parquet file. The Home view shows the active filename, row and column counts when available, data-quality summaries, and a row preview.
  3. Open Ask Queries.
  4. Enter a concrete question that uses columns in the file, for example:

What is the total revenue by country?

  1. Choose Ask, or press Ctrl+Enter on Linux and Windows (Command+Enter on macOS).

During the request, the desktop reports stages such as Analyzing data, Thinking, and Executing. A successful turn ends with an answer card and calculation evidence in the adjacent workspace. Generated Pandas code is available in Code. If Computation graph was enabled before the request, Graph is also available.

The full file is not uploaded in this workflow. The cloud receives your question and a compact file description containing schema and summary metadata; that description can include sample values. Generated code and optional graph artifacts return to the desktop, which computes the answer against the local file.

docs.title: Know the current boundary
docs.text:
The implemented capability covers descriptive analysis of one file, including aggregations, comparisons, rankings, historical trends, quality checks, transformations, and optional charts. Forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection are currently unavailable. nolainquery labels those requests as out of scope instead of presenting them as completed work.

Due to the generative nature of the label classifier, there might be cases in which a query involving one of those tasks is answered. However, the capabilities of the system are not thougt for giving such type of analysis, and therefore, such answers might be limited in their analysis.

Some schema-only questions, such as “What columns do I have?”, can be answered from the file description without generating code. An unrelated question gets a short refusal.

docs.title: If the first request does not complete
docs.text:
• Key rejected: see API key recovery.
  • No balance: see credit recovery.
  • Request refused: see unsupported and out-of-scope requests.
  • Service or execution failure: see service and runtime recovery.

You now have the shortest hosted workflow: a local file, a portal-issued key, and an answer computed on your device.

Continue with Desktop workflows to explore the rest of the implemented workspace, then read Credits before estimating ongoing use.

docs.title: Credits and model-call charges
docs.text: After a first query, the practical question is how much another query may use. nolainquery charges credits for language-model calls in the Cloud API. Running the returned code against your file on the local engine does not itself consume credits.

docs.title: How one model call is charged
docs.text:
The current billing configuration converts model cost into token credits at 1,000 credits per US dollar, rounding up. It then adds surplus credits, a configured service margin. The current surplus rate is 100%.

token_credits   = ceil(model_cost_usd × 1000)
surplus_credits = ceil(token_credits × 1.0)
charged_credits = token_credits + surplus_credits

For example, a model call costing $0.0026 produces 3 token credits after rounding. The current surplus adds 3 more, so the account is charged 6 credits. This example explains the formula; it is not a fixed per-call price.

The implementation records a charge after each completed model call. A single question may invoke several calls for intent classification, ambiguity analysis, code generation, graph compilation, visualization formatting, repair, or optional answer framing. Calls completed before a failure or cancellation remain chargeable. Polling the status of work already started does not create a model charge.

docs.title: Which requests can avoid a charge
docs.text:
A response that never invokes a model does not create a model-call charge. Some schema-only answers, such as a locally available column list or row count, can take that path. Most conversation turns use at least the intent classifier, including turns eventually judged off-topic or out of scope.

Clarification is not a flat charge of its own. The model calls used to detect ambiguity are charged, and the clarified request may trigger further calls.

docs.title: What the plan numbers currently mean
docs.text:
The repository declares monthly plan constants of 1,000 credits for free and 50,000 credits for premium. The website displays those amounts as UTC-month plan allowances.

However, the current repository contains no automated monthly grant or reset job that applies those constants to accounts. New profile balances default to zero in the database schema. Treat the displayed monthly amounts as configured plan targets, not as verified automatic grants, until grant automation is implemented. The balance shown in the portal and the desktop Settings badge is the amount currently available to spend.

docs.title: How additional capacity works today
docs.text:
The Cloud API has an implemented Stripe backend: it can create a validated Checkout Session for a configured package, and its signed webhook can add the purchased credits to an account.

That backend is not connected to a self-service purchase control in the current portal. The portal’s Subscription and Top Up tabs both direct users to contact the nolainquery team; the Top Up page explicitly says self-service top-ups are unavailable. Do not expect those tabs to open Stripe Checkout yet.

docs.title: What measured queries cost
docs.text:
The query-cost benchmark measured three 50-question runs on hard retail-invoice questions:

  • GPT-5.6 Luna with Pandas code only averaged 4.08 charged credits per question.
  • DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 with Pandas code only averaged 2.76.
  • GPT-5.6 Luna with Pandas plus a computation graph averaged 38.84.

These figures are descriptive measurements, not estimates guaranteed for a new file. They include worker calls but exclude conversation-side classification, semantic reading, and optional answer framing, so an interactive turn can cost more. The runs also differed in retry and success rates and had no ground-truth answers. In that sample, enabling the computation graph was the largest visible cost increase.

For your own recent activity, Settings → Query usage aggregates locally stored token counts and answer times over one day, seven days, or 30 days. Those token charts are usage evidence, not the authoritative account balance; use the credit badge or portal balance for the latter.

You can now distinguish verified per-call charging, measured query costs, and plan amounts that are not yet automatically granted. See Troubleshooting for a zero-credit response, or continue with How nolainquery is built to understand why planning is remote while execution stays local.

docs.title: Desktop workflows
docs.text: Once a file and API key are ready, the desktop provides several task-focused views. Home opens and previews data, Know Your Data builds exploratory charts, Ask Queries generates calculations, Pinned collects useful evidence, and Settings controls generation and shows local usage history.

docs.title: Open, preview, and switch datasets
docs.text:
Open Home and choose Choose dataset. The current file chooser supports .csv and .parquet. After the local engine reads the file, Home shows:

  • the active filename and available row and column counts
  • data-quality cards for properties such as completeness and duplicates
  • a paginated row preview
  • recently opened files for quick switching

Choose a data-quality card to read its explanation. Use Change file or a recent-file entry to switch the active dataset. The app keeps the file path; the full file remains on the device.

From the active-dataset strip, Ask about this data opens Ask Queries with a starter question, while Explore columns opens Know Your Data.

docs.title: Explore columns without writing a query
docs.text:
Know Your Data reads a local summary and groups columns by inferred semantic type. Search the column list, then select a column to add a chart tile. The app chooses an initial chart and aggregation from the column type.

Each tile can change its chart, aggregation, distribution coverage, or comparison column where those controls apply. Drag across a chart to zoom and double-click it to reset. Ask carries the selected column into Ask Queries, and Pin sends a completed tile to the Pinned view. Tile choices are saved locally for that file; Clear all removes the open exploration tiles.

This view performs deterministic local exploration. It does not require the Cloud API to invent a query, although the local Python engine must be running.

docs.title: Ask a question and follow the answer
docs.text:
Open Ask Queries, enter a concrete request, and choose Ask or press Ctrl+Enter (Command+Enter on macOS). For example:

Compare total revenue by country and show the five largest values.

The conversation panel preserves recent chats locally. Use New for a fresh thread, or select an earlier thread to return to its messages and artifacts. A thread can save up to ten analysis artifacts; after that, create a new conversation.

For an analysis request, the desktop sends the question and compact file metadata to the Cloud API, receives generated Pandas code and optional artifacts, then executes the calculation through the local engine. The answer card presents the result and can expose recipe steps that lead to the relevant code cell or graph node. Full result export is available as CSV; transformation artifacts preserve the active source format when supported by the export path.

If nolainquery asks what a term means, select an interpretation for each term and submit it. The chosen meanings accompany the resumed request. Choose the rephrase option when none of the choices matches your intent.

docs.title: Inspect code and run notebook cells
docs.text:
Every successful generated analysis can expose Code as calculation evidence. The code view divides generated Python into notebook-style cells at top-level section comments. Each cell has its own run button and displays its result, variables, execution time, or a user-facing error.

Cells share a persistent local session, so later cells can use variables created by earlier ones. The initial answer execution runs the generated cells from top to bottom in a fresh session. A later manual cell run does not automatically run its prerequisites, so rerun dependent cells in order when needed. The current code view has no separate Run all cells control.

The notebook is an inspection and execution surface for generated code, not a general-purpose hosted notebook. Code runs in the local engine’s restricted Pandas executor, and safety-blocked operations do not run.

docs.title: Add and inspect a computation graph
docs.text:
Before asking, enable Computation graph in the query composer. The Cloud API then attempts to compile an additional directed acyclic graph (DAG): a visual sequence of calculation operations and dependencies.

When compilation succeeds, Graph appears beside Code. You can inspect nodes, auto-layout the graph, execute it locally, enter Edit graph mode, add operations, and save the graph as DAG JSON. Graph compilation is optional, can fail while the Pandas result succeeds, and adds model calls; the measured cost difference is described in Credits.

When an answer includes a visualization specification, a Dashboard evidence tab renders the resulting chart. This generated dashboard is distinct from the deterministic chart tiles in Know Your Data.

docs.title: Collect evidence on the Pinned canvas
docs.text:
Use the pin control on a chart, generated graph, or generated code artifact to add it to Pinned. The Pinned view is a local canvas for arranging evidence from the active dataset and returning to its source answer. Pinning does not publish or upload the artifact.

Only completed artifact types supported by the current pinning controls can be added. An unavailable pin control means that view has no pinnable artifact yet.

docs.title: Configure implemented generation features
docs.text:
Open Settings → Capabilities & plans to control locally stored generation preferences:

  • Execution plan: Automatic selects the default implemented Pandas plan. Ibis is a placeholder and is not selectable as a working engine.
  • Allow visualization requests: when disabled, chart or plot requests are blocked locally with guidance to enable the setting or ask for a table.
  • Allow transformation requests: when disabled, cleaning, reshaping, and export-copy requests are blocked before generation.

The Computation graph switch remains in Ask Queries because a graph is an optional artifact, not a separate execution plan.

docs.title: Read local usage history
docs.text:
Settings → Query usage combines usage attached to saved conversations with locally persisted generation records. It shows:

  • input and output tokens for the last query and selected period
  • cumulative token charts for the last day, seven days, or 30 days
  • last-query time, recent and period averages, and query counts

When the Cloud API reports model time, the app uses it; otherwise it falls back to elapsed wall-clock time from question to answer. Older turns may show no token counts. These metrics stay in desktop local storage and are not a billing ledger or a replacement for the account credit balance.

You can now move from file inspection to local exploration, generated analysis, auditable evidence, and usage review. Read Credits before choosing costlier graph workflows, and keep Troubleshooting nearby for visible recovery steps.

docs.title: Troubleshoot the desktop workflow
docs.text: Use the message visible in the desktop or Cloud API response to choose a recovery path. These steps stay on the user side: they restore a normal workflow without exposing service credentials, database checks, or maintainer operations.

docs.title: The API key is missing or rejected
docs.text:
Visible symptom: Ask Queries says No API key configured, Settings says No API key set. Queries will be blocked, or a request reports a missing or invalid API key.

  1. Open Settings.
  2. Paste an active key from nolainquery.com/account.
  3. Choose Save API Key.
  4. Wait for the status badge to show the tier and balance before retrying.

If the key was revoked, lost, or is still rejected, revoke it in Account → API Keys, create a new key, and save the replacement in the desktop. The portal shows a full key only at creation time.

docs.title: The service returns 402 or no credits
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the badge says No credits remaining, or the Cloud API returns HTTP 402 with either a zero-balance message or a message that the key is not linked to a portal account.

  • For an unlinked key, sign in at nolainquery.com, create the key under your own Account → API Keys, and save that key in Settings.
  • For a linked key with zero balance, confirm the balance in the portal. The current Subscription and Top Up tabs direct users to contact the nolainquery team; self-service top-ups are not available in the portal yet.

Retry only after Settings shows a positive balance. The plan’s displayed monthly amount does not prove that credits were granted; see Credits.

docs.title: The request is unsupported or out of scope
docs.text:
Visible symptom: nolainquery says the request cannot be done with the available capabilities, refuses an unrelated question, or Settings reports that visualization or transformation requests are disabled.

The current capability performs descriptive analysis of one loaded file. Ask for historical summaries, comparisons, rankings, distributions, data quality, cleaning, reshaping, or a chart. Forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection are unavailable.

For example, replace:

Forecast next quarter's revenue.

with an implemented descriptive request:

Show monthly historical revenue and compare the latest quarter with the previous quarter.

If a chart or transformation was blocked locally, open Settings → Capabilities & plans, enable the corresponding feature, save, and submit the request again. Otherwise keep the feature disabled and rephrase the request as a table or descriptive analysis.

docs.title: Intent classification returns 503
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the request returns HTTP 503 with a message such as Intent classification failed, or reports that the language-model service is unavailable.

The Cloud API could not classify the conversation turn, so no analysis job was accepted. Wait briefly and retry the same request once. If the failure continues, verify that the hosted site itself is reachable and contact support with the approximate time and the visible error text. Do not include your API key or file contents.

docs.title: The desktop cannot reach a service
docs.text:
Three services participate in a normal query: the desktop UI, the local Python engine that reads and executes the file, and the Cloud API that generates the calculation.

Local engine unreachable or connection refused

Restart the desktop launcher. A source run is ready only after its terminal prints Local execution engine is ready. If port 8001 is already occupied, stop the other engine process before starting ./launch.sh again.

Cloud API unreachable or request failed to fetch

Confirm that the machine is online. For a source build using the hosted service, restart it from the repository root with:

VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=https://nolainquery.com ./launch.sh

A plain development launch defaults to a Cloud API on http://127.0.0.1:8000, so it will fail unless a maintainer has started the local cloud stack.

Cloud API online, but generation runtime unavailable

The API is reachable but cannot queue generation work. Hosted users should retry later and contact support if it persists. Maintainers running the local stack should use the private Cloud API development guide; the desktop cannot repair Redis or the generation worker.

docs.title: The app asks for clarification
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the conversation shows Clarification needed and offers interpretations for one or more terms.

This is a request for intent, not an execution failure. Select one meaning for each term and submit the choices. nolainquery sends those meanings with the resumed request and uses them when generating the calculation.

If no option matches, choose the rephrase action and rewrite the original question with an explicit definition. For example, change “top customers” to “the five customers with the highest total revenue.” The clarified request may make additional model calls and consume more credits.

docs.title: Local execution fails and repair runs out
docs.text:
Visible symptom: progress reaches Repairing generated code, then the answer reports that it could not compute a result, generated code was blocked for safety, a column was not found, or the generation attempt ceiling was exhausted.

The desktop reports a local Pandas error to the Cloud API, which can generate a repair. The current configuration limits sandbox, syntax, and local-runtime repair attempts; it does not retry indefinitely.

Use the narrowest matching action:

  1. For an unknown column, return to Home and copy the exact column name into the question.
  2. For a format-loading error, reopen a supported .csv or .parquet file.
  3. For a safety block, remove requests for filesystem, network, package, or process access and ask only for a calculation over the loaded data.
  4. For a complex failure, split the request into a smaller calculation, verify that result, then ask a follow-up.
  5. If Pandas produced a valid answer but only graph compilation failed, turn off Computation graph and retry without that optional artifact.

Completed model calls from failed and repaired attempts can still consume credits. Repeating the identical request many times is therefore less useful than changing the column name, scope, or optional graph setting.

docs.title: The selected file does not appear
docs.text:
The current desktop chooser lists only .csv and .parquet. Although the local preprocessing code contains Excel handlers, .xlsx and .xls are not exposed in the current chooser and should not be treated as a supported desktop first-use path. Convert the workbook to CSV or Parquet, then reopen it.

Once the visible symptom is resolved, return to Desktop workflows. For the system boundaries behind these failures, continue with How nolainquery is built.

docs.title: Try the desktop app from source
docs.text: This is the shortest public path for running the Linux desktop app from this repository while using the hosted Cloud API. It starts the user interface and the local Python execution engine; it does not require private Cloud API credentials.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
This setup script targets Debian or Ubuntu. You need:

  • a Linux desktop with apt, internet access, and permission to use sudo
  • Git, because the setup script does not install it
  • a Google account and a portal-issued API key from Ask your first question with nolainquery

The script installs the Tauri system libraries, Rust when absent, Node.js 20 when npm is absent, Python dependencies in .venv, and frontend packages. On another Linux distribution, install the equivalent Tauri prerequisites manually before continuing. Windows installers are a separate distribution path; macOS support is planned and is not available from these scripts.

docs.title: Clone and prepare the repository
docs.text:
Run these commands in a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/jdvillegasg/nolain-query.git
cd nolain-query
./setup.sh

Setup is complete when the script prints Everything is ready!. The command downloads packages and may ask for your system password while apt installs dependencies.

docs.title: Start the desktop against the hosted API
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=https://nolainquery.com ./launch.sh

The launcher activates .venv, starts the local Python engine on port 8001, waits for its health check, and then starts the Tauri development window. The terminal prints Local execution engine is ready. before the desktop UI starts.

The explicit VITE_CLOUD_API_URL matters: a development build otherwise defaults to a Cloud API on http://127.0.0.1:8000. Leave this terminal running while using the app; Ctrl+C stops the UI and local engine.

docs.title: Verify the first run
docs.text:
1. Open Settings, paste your portal API key, and choose Save API Key.
  2. Confirm that the status badge shows a tier and a positive credit balance.
  3. Open Home, choose a .csv or .parquet file, and confirm that the data preview appears.
  4. Open Ask Queries and ask a descriptive question about a real column.

The run is successful when an answer card appears and Code shows the Pandas calculation executed against your local file.

docs.title: If startup fails
docs.text:
• .venv not found: rerun ./setup.sh from the repository root.
  • A required command is missing: rerun setup and resolve the first dependency error it reports.
  • Port 8001 is already in use: stop the other local engine, then rerun the launcher.
  • The engine exits or never becomes ready: use the terminal’s first Python error as the cause; the desktop cannot execute files until the engine starts.

For user-facing query failures, use Troubleshooting. Maintainers who intentionally need a fully local Cloud API can follow Cloud API development setup and the repository’s scripts/launch-cloud-dev.sh; that path requires private service configuration and Docker.

With the desktop and local engine running, continue with Desktop workflows.

docs.title: Clarifications
docs.text:
A question like “top countries by revenue” is clear English and still underspecified for a file. Revenue might be Quantity * Price, or a column that already holds a total. “Top” might mean a count, a percentile, or a threshold. This chapter is how nolainquery decides whether to ask, what to ask, and how the answer is used — without gluing that answer onto the question as extra prose.

If you have not read A conversation from start to finish, start there. This chapter is the clarification turn in detail.

docs.title: What a clarification is
docs.text:
A clarification is a pause in the Ask Queries loop. Semantic reading has found a term whose mapping onto the sketch is not unique. The desktop shows the term, a short reason, and a short list of interpretations, always ending with Other (please specify). You pick one meaning. Generation then continues with that meaning treated as settled.

The product asks only when the fork would change the calculation. A choice between a normal group-by and a normal sum is not a clarification; the Planner can take that on its own.

docs.title: The three-stage pipeline
docs.text:
Semantic reading is a three-stage pass (SemanticAgent).

  1. Noun chunks (spaCy). The question is split into atomic phrases. Filter values (France, £50), interrogatives, and aggregation heads (“average”, “total”) are dropped. Adjectives such as “top” are kept separately as modifiers.
  2. Schema-grounded routing. Each surviving noun is compared to the sketch — column names plus type, description, and sample values — using vector similarity. Match count picks a specialist:
  3. no column match → granularity (unit of analysis)
  4. several matches → polysemy (which column)
  5. one match → aggregation path (what to compute)
  6. adjective → modifier (how to operationalise “top”, “recent”, …)
  7. Specialists, then merge. The four specialists run in parallel. If one of them fails, the others still stand. Only if all invoked specialists fail does the turn fall back to “please rephrase.” Findings are then deduplicated by term, ranked (polysemy first), and capped (default: two questions). Asking four things before a first result is where people leave.

spaCy is loaded once per process. Agent instances are reused per model, so a conversation turn does not pay a fresh model load.

Similarity cutoffs and the cap live in cloud_api/app/config/generation.yaml (semantic_similarity_threshold, semantic_column_match_threshold, semantic_max_concepts).

When spaCy is missing, a single open-ended prompt replaces stages 1–2. That path still merges and caps.

docs.title: The session glossary
docs.text:
A chosen meaning is stored on the conversation session (resolved_clarifications). It is a glossary for this file and this session, not a note attached to one question. If you have already said that revenue means Quantity * Price, the next unrelated question on the same session will not ask again.

Newer choices override the same term. A new session starts empty. Terms are matched by lemma, not by substring: a resolved “order” does not silence a later “reorder rate.”

docs.title: API fields and prompt fields
docs.text:
The conversation API receives choices as clarifications[].chosen_interpretation. The choice is not appended to the question as [Clarification: 'revenue' means '…']. The query string stays the query. The resolved pairs travel as a structured field on the worker config (clarifications), then into a dedicated prompt slot ({clarifications}) as JSON:

[{"term": "revenue", "means": "Quantity * Price"}]

Empty means (none). Custom text from Other (please specify) is length-limited and stripped of control characters and newlines before it is stored or sent to a model. The generate and repair prompts treat that JSON as user-supplied data that defines terms — not as instructions.

On the desktop, Rephrase question puts the original question back in the Conversation Input so you can edit it. It does not discard the wording.

docs.title: Shortcut
docs.text: When the desktop resends with a clarifications payload, classification and semantic reading are skipped. The meaning is treated as settled; the server admits the Plan with the current graph and chart toggles.

docs.title: Fallbacks and tuning boundaries
docs.text:
If spaCy is unavailable or deterministic parsing fails, a single open-ended model call replaces parsing and routing. If every invoked specialist fails, or that fallback cannot produce a valid result, the conversation asks the user to rephrase and does not generate.

Three current settings tune detection rather than change the product contract: candidate deduplication similarity, schema-column match similarity, and the maximum number of concepts shown (default two). Raising recall can create more interruptions; tightening the thresholds can miss real ambiguity. The stable boundary is that clarification is reserved for choices that can materially change the calculation.

The next chapter, How a Plan is declared, explains the verified dependency recipe used after the question’s meaning is settled.

docs.title: A conversation from start to finish
docs.text:
The last two chapters explained the design and named the parts. This chapter is the desktop product in motion: what happens, request by request, from the moment you load a file to the moment a table (and maybe a chart) appears.

The path described here is Ask Queries. There is a second door — direct generation without a chat — that covers only the middle of this story (produce artifacts, poll, execute). It does not classify, clarify, or repair. Both doors produce the same Capability. This chapter is the full loop.

You will see HTTP paths. They are the messages on the wire, not the entry point for the ideas. The ideas are: open a session on a sketch, decide what kind of turn this is, maybe generate, execute locally, report back, repair if needed, optionally narrate.

docs.title: The loop at a glance
docs.text:
Seven moves. The rest of the chapter walks each one, then shows what changes if the question is off-topic, ambiguous, or fails on the real file.

  1. Start a session with the current sketch. No model call, no charge.
  2. Send the question (and your graph/chart toggles). The server classifies the turn and either replies immediately or admits a generation job.
  3. Poll the job until artifacts are ready (or the job fails).
  4. Execute locally on the engine that has the file.
  5. Report the outcome. On success, the result is stored for follow-ups. On failure with budget remaining, the server queues a repair.
  6. If repairing, poll and execute again until the run succeeds or the budget is exhausted.
  7. Optionally ask for a narrative wrapping of the numbers.

Three kinds of Pandas retry are configured separately. Generation and repair calls are also bounded by a chain-wide ceiling (default 9):

Kind When Where it happens Sandbox retry Truncated, empty, or statically illegal code during cloud generation Inside the worker, before anything ships Syntax repair Deterministic delimiter repair cannot make generated code parse Inside the worker; separate default budget of 1 Runtime repair Code passed those checks but failed when executed locally After you report the error; a new job, no new classification

Compiler and chart retries use another budget and do not participate in the local report-and-repair loop.

docs.title: What you need before the first message
docs.text:
• The desktop has asked the local engine for a sketch (GET http://localhost:8001/data_summary?source_path=...).
  • Requests carry a valid API key (X-API-Key).
  • Sessions are reused until the desktop resets local state. On the server they expire after 24 hours.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the loaded file has columns Invoice, Quantity, Price, Country, and you ask:

What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?

You have left both toggles on: compile a computation graph, and produce a chart.

docs.title: 1. Start a session
docs.text:
The desktop posts the sketch and receives a session_id. Nothing is classified. Nothing is charged. Redis now holds conversation:{session_id} — a short-lived thread bound to that sketch.

POST /api/v1/conversation/start
X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{"metadata":{"available_columns":["Invoice","Quantity","Price","Country"]}}

docs.title: 2. Send the question
docs.text:
The desktop posts the session id, the question, the sketch, and the toggles. Without a clarification payload, the conversation graph runs:

POST /api/v1/conversation/message
X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{"session_id":"SESSION_ID","message":"What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?","metadata":{"available_columns":["Invoice","Quantity","Price","Country"]},"compile_dag":true,"include_visualization":true}
  1. Classify the turn (one model call). For this question the kind is a data question.
  2. Read the wording for ambiguities (semantic analysis). “Revenue” might mean Quantity * Price, or it might mean something else in your file. If the reading is ambiguous, you get a clarification and the loop waits. If it fails, you get a text reply and no job.
  3. If the reading is clear, policy admits the Pandas Plan with your toggles and queues a worker job.

If the classifier cannot run or its output is unusable, this request returns HTTP 503. The gate does not fail open into generation.

The response type tells the desktop what to do next:

Response type Meaning What the desktop does text_response Off-topic, unsafe, underspecified, explanation, out of scope, or fallback Show the text meta_answer Question about the file’s structure Show the metadata answer clarification Ambiguous terms Resend with your chosen interpretations generation Job accepted Poll task_id

A generation response also echoes capability_id, plan_id, and the toggles the server actually admitted, so the desktop can show what was queued.

Clarification shortcut. When you resend with clarifications filled in, classification and semantic reading are skipped. The meaning of the question is treated as settled; the server queues the Plan with the current toggles. How terms are detected, stored as a session glossary, and passed into generation is in Clarifications.

What the classifier is allowed to do. It chooses the kind of turn. For generation kinds it may suggest a Capability and a Plan from the live catalog. It does not turn the graph or the chart on or off. Those are your toggles. Policy, not the prompt, rebuilds the pipeline.

docs.title: 3. Poll the job
docs.text:
The desktop asks for status about every 1.5 seconds. When the pipeline status is success or failed, the job is done.

The payload that matters for the rest of the loop:

  • pandas_code — the program to run locally
  • optional graph (the API field for the public computation graph, internally the dag artifact) and visualization_spec — if you asked for them and those stations succeeded
  • pandas_retries_left — remaining local repair jobs
  • pandas_sandbox_retries_left — remaining in-cloud static retries
  • pandas_attempts_used / pandas_total_max_attempts — chain-wide usage and ceiling
  • billing.charged_credits — running total for worker model calls
  • generation_attempts — per-call diagnostics (finish reason, selected repair profile, tokens, accepted or rejected)

While the job runs, the worker may retry writing the code internally (truncated completion, empty extract, static sandbox reject). Partial length-limited code is never sent for execution.

docs.title: 4. Execute locally
docs.text:
Execution is on the local engine (port 8001), never on the Cloud API:

  • run the Pandas code against the loaded file
  • if a graph artifact is present, run that too

No cloud credit is charged for this step. This is the first moment the analysis meets the rows.

docs.title: 5. Report the outcome
docs.text:
After every local run — success or failure — the desktop tells the conversation what happened, so follow-up questions have execution context.

Success. The server stores the result and returns { "status": "ok" }. Later, “how did you calculate that?” can be answered from this memory without generating again.

Failure with budget remaining. If the error and the failed code are both present, the previous job succeeded on the cloud side (it shipped code), and pandas_retries_left is still positive, the server:

  1. Reads the remaining budget from that job
  2. Queues a new generate-and-repair job with the failed code and the error (no new classifier, no new semantic turn)
  3. Decrements the runtime-repair budget on the new job
  4. Resets the in-cloud sandbox budget for that repair (so a depleted sandbox count cannot block a new attempt) and carries the chain-wide attempt count forward (so repairs cannot multiply forever)
  5. Returns { "status": "repairing", "task_id": "..." }

The desktop then repeats poll → execute → report with the new task id. If no retries remain, the server returns { "status": "ok" } and the desktop keeps the error.

Repair settings are chosen from the kind of failure and the retry index (syntax vs runtime vs truncation, first try vs repeated signature). All Pandas generate-or-repair calls remain bounded by the chain-wide ceiling.

docs.title: 6. Optional narrative
docs.text: After a successful execution, the desktop may ask the cloud to frame the numbers as a short paragraph. That is another model call, charged if it runs. If it fails, the endpoint still returns an empty narrative: you keep the table.

docs.title: The same loop, other kinds of turn
docs.text:
The revenue question was the happy path. Dialogue exists so that not every message takes it.

What you asked What the server does Credits “What’s the weather?” / jailbreak / “analyze my data” Classify → text reply Charged if that path called a model “What columns do I have?” Classify → answer from the sketch The normal path includes the classifier model call “How did you calculate that?” Classify → grounded text from stored result Charged if that path called a model “Forecast next quarter’s sales” Classify or safety net → named refusal Charged if that path called a model Clear data question Classify → semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Ambiguous data question Classify → semantic reading → clarification Per model call already made Your reply to a clarification Skip classify/semantic → generation Per model call in the job “That doesn’t look right” Always semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Local Pandas error, retries left Report → repair job Per model call in the repair job Local execution Desktop port 8001 No cloud charge Answer framing Optional synthesize Per model call

A classifier outage or invalid classifier response is different from a normal text branch: the message request returns HTTP 503 and queues no job.

Worker cost details and Plan station lists: The parts of the system.

docs.title: What the product will and will not do
docs.text:
• Data questions — including charts and reshape — admit the Pandas Plan. Charts set the visualization toggle; they do not change which Plan you are on.
  • Requests no registered Capability can serve return a text message naming what is available, and do not admit generation. A wording-based safety net still catches forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection while only descriptive analysis is enabled.
  • Explanation requests use saved result context and do not queue generation.

docs.title: The HTTP surface, as a table
docs.text:
Once the story is clear, the endpoints are just names for the moves:

Endpoint Move POST /api/v1/conversation/start Open a session on a sketch POST /api/v1/conversation/message Classify (or skip) and maybe admit a job GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} Poll generation POST /api/v1/conversation/result Store the local outcome; maybe queue repair POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize Optional narrative GET /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Read the session DELETE /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Delete the session POST /api/v1/cancel_task/{task_id} Cooperative cancel between stages

Session read and delete use the same owned-session check as message, result, and synthesize. A missing session returns 404; a different API key returns 403. Status and cancellation also enforce job ownership. Model calls already completed keep their charges.

Request bodies, response shapes, and curl examples: Calling the Cloud API. Job diagnostics, attempt logs, and credit receipts are listed in that chapter's status payload section.

Next, Clarifications explains why the system pauses, how its three-stage semantic pipeline works, and how a selected meaning reaches generation without rewriting the user’s question.

docs.title: How a Plan is declared
docs.text:
The last three chapters treated a Plan as a kitchen line: an ordered sequence of stations that consume and produce artifacts. This short chapter is the recipe card for that line — a YAML file that answers one question: in what order must artifacts exist?

Use this as a concise reference for what the current YAML declares and what Python adds at runtime. Product decisions — whether a station is optional, whether its artifact appears on the canvas — do not live in YAML.

docs.title: What the file is
docs.text:
Each YAML file in cloud_api/app/generation/plans/config/ declares one Plan. Every file uses the same schema; only the entries under artifacts differ.

At startup the Cloud API loads all of these files and registers each graph by the plan_id inside it. The file name is a convenience. Convention is {capability}.{engine}.yaml — for example data_analysis.pandas.yaml — but the authoritative id is the field in the file.

Think of the YAML as a bill of materials, not a program. It says “the computation graph depends on the Pandas code” the way a recipe says “the icing goes on after the cake.” It does not say “icing is optional if the guest declined dessert.” That second sentence is a request option, and request options are product behavior.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
plan_id: <capability>/<engine>
terminal_stage: <stage_id>        # always runs last; implemented in Python

artifacts:
  - kind: <artifact_kind>         # stable id this stage produces
    stage: <stage_id>             # station implementation id
    depends_on: [<artifact_kind>] # direct dependencies only (may be [])
Key Required Meaning plan_id yes Plan identifier; must match the Capability catalog terminal_stage yes Final station (persists results after per-call credit charges). Not listed under artifacts. artifacts yes Ordered list of station / artifact entries

Each artifacts entry:

Field Required Meaning kind yes Artifact kind produced by stage stage yes Registered station id on the Capability depends_on yes Artifact kinds that must exist before this station runs

Validation and other internal steps are ordinary entries in this list. The YAML does not mark them “internal.” Canvas visibility — whether the desktop shows the dish — is configured in plan_behavior.py, next to the catalog.

docs.title: Current data_analysis/pandas declaration
docs.text:
The checked-in YAML declares this dependency order:

Artifact kind Stage Direct dependency code_pandas generate_pandas none dag compile_dag code_pandas visualization_spec format_visualization code_pandas visualization_validation validate_visualization visualization_spec analysis validate_dag dag

finalize_plan is the terminal stage and is deliberately outside the artifacts list.

docs.title: Example: validating the graph
docs.text:
validate_dag checks the dag artifact and produces an internal analysis object the desktop never renders. In YAML that is only a dependency:

  - kind: analysis
    stage: validate_dag
    depends_on: [dag]

Whether this station runs at all depends on whether you asked for the graph. That gate is not in this file.

docs.title: How dependencies are interpreted
docs.text:
List only direct dependencies in depends_on. The loader checks that every referenced kind appears in the same file.

Independent branches (same depends_on) run in YAML list order once their dependencies are satisfied. If a dependency was requested but not produced — an optional station failed — dependent stations are skipped automatically rather than run on missing input.

docs.title: What Python adds
docs.text:
The loader rejects YAML entries that try to declare optional, request_option, or canvas. Python supplies those behaviors:

Stage or artifact Current Python behavior generate_pandas required compile_dag, validate_dag gated by compile_dag format_visualization, validate_visualization gated by include_visualization code_pandas, dag, visualization_spec exposed as canvas artifacts

The registry currently exposes data_analysis/pandas as implemented, selectable, and the default. It also exposes data_analysis/ibis as unimplemented and not selectable; there is no corresponding Ibis YAML recipe. Legacy six-part Plan ids are normalized to the Pandas Plan plus request options.

The conceptual chapters end here. Next, learn exactly what the local sketch can contain in Sketch and metadata, then use it in Calling the Cloud API.

docs.title: The parts of the system
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained why nolainquery is split the way it is. This chapter is a map of what sits on each side of that split: the desktop, the local engine, the Cloud API, and the generation pipeline that turns an admitted question into artifacts.

If you have not read The system philosophy, start there. The words Capability, Plan, Stage, artifact, sketch, and intent are used here with the meanings that chapter introduced.

This chapter defines the running components, their boundaries, the generation framework, retry budgets, and the repository map. The next chapter owns the request-by-request walkthrough.

docs.title: Two machines, one question
docs.text:
When you ask “What is total revenue by country?” two processes on your computer talk to a third process in the cloud.

The desktop app is what you see: file picker, question bar, results table, chart canvas. It does not compute the answer itself. It asks a local helper to describe the file, asks the Cloud API to produce a recipe, then asks the helper to run that recipe.

The local engine is that helper (a small Python service on port 8001). It is the only process that opens the file. It derives the sketch (column names, types, summaries, samples) and later executes the artifacts the cloud returned.

The Cloud API is the remote reasoning service (port 8000 in development). It never receives the file. It receives the question plus the sketch, decides whether to generate anything, and — if so — returns artifacts.

Around the Cloud API sit four supporting services:

  • Redis — short-lived memory for conversation sessions and generation jobs.
  • A background worker (Celery) — runs the Plan’s stages so the HTTP server does not block on model calls.
  • Supabase — who you are, whether your key is valid, how many credits remain.
  • OpenRouter — the single gateway for every language-model call. The product does not speak to OpenAI, DeepSeek, or anyone else directly.

A health endpoint (GET /health) reports whether Redis, the worker, and Supabase are reachable. Generation refuses to start (503) if Redis or the worker is down.

docs.title: The generation framework
docs.text: The control plane does not have an open-ended “do data science” prompt. It has a menu, a kitchen line, stations, and dishes. Those four ideas are Capability, Plan, Stage, and Artifact.

docs.title: Menu, line, station, dish
docs.text:
A restaurant is a useful picture:

In the restaurant In nolainquery Today An item on the menu Capability — a product the cloud knows how to generate data_analysis: descriptive analysis of one CSV or Parquet file A kitchen line that prepares that item Plan — an engine: an ordered pipeline of stages data_analysis/pandas (implemented). data_analysis/ibis is on the menu but not staffed A station on that line Stage — a unit that consumes and produces artifacts Write the code; optionally compile a graph; optionally write a chart contract; validate; finish A dish that leaves a station Artifact — a typed output the desktop can use Executable Pandas code, optional computation graph, optional chart contract

A few consequences of this picture, which the rest of the system depends on:

  • Intent is not on the menu. Intent is the maître d’ deciding whether you sit down, get a glass of water from memory, or get sent to the kitchen. Mixing intent with Capability would let the maître d’ invent new dishes.
  • A chart is a side, not a second menu item. You toggle it on the same Plan. There is no “visualization Plan.”
  • Semantic analysis is a conversation with the waiter, before the ticket reaches the kitchen. It is not a Capability.
  • The chef does not redesign the line. Policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and from your toggles (the admission step in cloud_api/app/generation/policy.py).

Optional artifacts on the Pandas Plan:

Your toggle What you get Compile DAG (default on) A computation-graph artifact (dag) Dashboard / chart (default on) A chart contract (visualization_spec)

The live menu is GET /api/v1/capabilities. Capabilities register themselves when the generation package loads.

docs.title: What the Pandas line produces
docs.text:
The primary dish is always executable analysis (code_pandas, returned to clients as pandas_code). Everything else is optional and derived.

Station Consumes Produces Calls a model? Optional? Write Pandas code — code_pandas Yes No. Static sandbox check; no execution on the server Compile DAG code_pandas dag Yes Yes, if you asked for the graph Format visualization code_pandas visualization_spec Yes Yes, if you asked for a chart Validate visualization visualization_spec internal check No With the chart Validate DAG dag internal check No With the graph Finalize code_pandas — No No. Persists produced artifacts after per-call charges

Dependencies between stations — “the graph cannot be compiled before the code exists” — are declared in a YAML recipe card. That card is the subject of How a Plan is declared. Whether a station is optional, and whether its dish appears on the canvas, is a product decision and lives next to the catalog, not in the recipe.

When code is regenerated (sandbox retry or runtime repair), derived dishes are thrown away and cooked again if you still asked for them. An old graph attached to new code would lie about what ran.

docs.title: How many model calls a job tends to make
docs.text:
These counts are the worker stations only. Classification and semantic reading, if they ran, are extra conversation-side calls.

Options Typical worker model calls Pandas only 1 (+ repairs if local execution fails) Pandas + graph 2 (code + compile); extra retries are separate budgets Pandas + chart, no graph 2 Pandas + graph + chart 3 or more

docs.title: Retry budgets
docs.text:
Retries are not one pool. Each failure mode has a different fix, so each has its own budget (configured in cloud_api/app/config/generation.yaml):

Budget Spent when Default Sandbox retries The worker rejects truncated, empty, or statically illegal code before it ships 2 Syntax-repair retries Generated code still has invalid syntax after deterministic delimiter repair 1 Runtime-repair jobs The code shipped, the desktop ran it, and the real file threw an error 2 Compile / chart retries Graph or chart compilation or validation failed 2 Chain-wide ceiling Any Pandas generate-or-repair call, across the whole chain 9

A repair selects a profile by the kind of failure (syntax, Unicode, sandbox policy, runtime, truncation, …) and how many times it has already been tried. Surgical categories emit with reasoning disabled so hidden tokens cannot empty the completion. Runtime-repair jobs get a fresh sandbox budget so a depleted in-cloud budget cannot block a new attempt; they inherit the chain-wide attempt count so nested jobs cannot multiply forever.

docs.title: Dialogue boundary
docs.text:
Conversation routes sit in front of generation. A normal message incurs a classifier model call even when the final branch is a metadata answer, refusal, or explanation. If classification or its model fails, the route returns HTTP 503; no fail-open generation occurs. Clarification replies are the explicit shortcut: they bypass classification and semantic analysis and proceed to server-side Plan admission.

The classifier may suggest a registered Capability and Plan, but policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and client options. The concrete branches and their HTTP responses belong in A conversation from start to finish.

docs.title: Authentication and credits, in one paragraph
docs.text: Every workflow endpoint requires an API key (X-API-Key). Conversation routes check that credits remain without charging; each model call is charged the moment it completes. Portal-linked keys with an empty balance return HTTP 402. Unlinked non-developer keys return 402. Unlinked owner developer keys skip credit checks. Details: Credits. Portal account routes (/api/auth/*) use a Supabase sign-in token instead of the API key.

docs.title: Job memory
docs.text:
A generation job lives in Redis for one hour (job_state:{job_id}). A conversation session lives for 24 hours (conversation:{session_id}). The desktop polls GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} for progress. Useful statuses include queued, generating_code, compiling_from_code, formatting_visualization, validating, finalizing, success, failed, and cancelled. Cancellation is cooperative between stages; model calls already completed stay charged.

How to read a job — retries, token totals, credit receipts, worker logs — is covered in Calling the Cloud API and maintainer documentation (docs-private/).

docs.title: Two APIs for the same Capability
docs.text:
Door What it is for Conversation (/api/v1/conversation/*) The desktop product: session, classification, clarification, local repair Direct generation (POST /api/v2/generate_dag) The same Capability without a chat: admit, synthesize, return artifacts Legacy (POST /api/v1/generate_dag) An older planner → compiler chain that does not use the Capability registry

Other useful endpoints: the model catalog (GET /api/v1/llm/models), the Capability catalog (GET /api/v1/capabilities), and standalone semantic analysis (POST /api/v1/analyze_query). Full request shapes and curl examples: Calling the Cloud API.

docs.title: Current product boundary
docs.text: out_of_scope is doing real work: the classifier sees the live catalog, and anything the catalog cannot serve returns a text message and does not admit generation. The Ibis Plan is the next engine for the same product, not a second product. It is catalogued and rejected until implemented.

docs.text:
This table is a lookup, not a starting point. Ideas in this chapter come first; these are the files that implement them.
